profile.summary: MULAN is a protein language model that reads a protein's sequence together with its three-dimensional structure, and returns per-residue or whole-protein embeddings. The structure enters as backbone and side-chain torsion angles, handled by a small added module called the Structure Adapter, whose output is added to the embeddings of a pretrained ESM-2 model that is then fine-tuned. The embeddings are meant to be used as features for downstream predictors.

summary_quotes.text: MULAN has a pre-trained sequence encoder and an introduced parameter-efficient Structure Adapter, which are then fused and trained together.
It consists of an MLP that projects residue angles to embeddings with dimension h, followed by a Transformer layer with rotary positional embeddings (Su et al. 2024).
Finally, angle embeddings are added to initial ESM2’s residue embeddings.
Run inference** to extract residue-level embeddings from the last layer of MULAN.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MULAN keeps a pretrained ESM-2 encoder and adds a Structure Adapter: an MLP that turns each residue's torsion angles into an embedding, followed by one Transformer layer with rotary position embeddings. Each residue is described by the backbone angles phi and psi and up to five side-chain chi angles, with missing values filled by a reserved padding value. The angle embeddings are added to ESM-2's residue embeddings and the whole model is fine-tuned with the masked language modelling objective of ESM-2, masking 15% of tokens, and masking angles along with their residues. For AlphaFold2 structures, angles of residues with low confidence are masked.

quotes.text: MULAN has a pre-trained sequence encoder and an introduced parameter-efficient Structure Adapter, which are then fused and trained together.
which results in an angle vector [ϕ,ψ,χ1,χ2,χ3,χ4,χ5] for each residue.
It consists of an MLP that projects residue angles to embeddings with dimension h, followed by a Transformer layer with rotary positional embeddings (Su et al. 2024).
Finally, angle embeddings are added to initial ESM2’s residue embeddings.
We utilize the same masked language modeling objective (MLM) (Devlin et al. 2018) as ESM2 for sequences, randomly masking 15% of tokens in a batch.
We show that it is useful to mask uncertain residues in AlphaFold2 structure models (with pLDDT >70) before passing them to the Structure Adapter

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are released on Hugging Face: MULAN-small, MULAN-ESM2-35M and MULAN-ESM2-650M. The paper names them MULAN S, M and L and gives 9M, 37M and 652M parameters, initialised from ESM-2 8M, 35M and 650M; the Hugging Face parameter counts of the files read here are 9,077,010, 36,769,870 and 672,047,862. The Hugging Face listing for this author holds only these three models, so the SaProt-initialised variants the repository describes are not published there. The README records a change on 31/03/2025 that added the medium and large checkpoints, updated MULAN-small and moved the code to rotary position embeddings, so a result should name both the checkpoint revision and the code commit.

sections.title: What it is for
sections.body: MULAN produces embeddings, not scores. The repository extracts residue-level embeddings from the last layer and suggests mean pooling for a protein-level embedding; downstream predictors are then trained on those embeddings. The authors evaluate on nine downstream tasks and report the largest gains for protein-protein interaction prediction.

strengths.text: Cheap to produce and to run: the structure module adds about 0.3% of the parameters of the large model, and the authors report fine-tuning in up to three days on one GPU.

quotes.text: It adds just 0.3% parameter overhead to ESM2 L (652M parameters), compared to PST’s 69% and S-PLM’s 13.8%.
it requires only brief finetuning (up to 3 days on one GPU) instead of months of training for models like ProstT5, ESM3, and SaProt.

strengths.text: Structure enters as torsion angles, which the authors note are rotation and translation invariant and therefore easy to use inside a transformer.

quotes.text: The residue torsion angles are rotation- and translation-invariant; thus, they are easy to use inside a transformer model.

run_guide.summary: Install the repository at a pinned commit, load a released MULAN checkpoint and extract residue embeddings for structures in a folder.
prerequisites: A folder of .pdb or .cif structures, one protein each. For experimental structures, repair them with pdbfixer first, in its own conda environment as the README describes.
The Foldseek binary only if using a SaProt-initialised model; with ESM-2 based MULAN it can be skipped by passing extract_foldseek_in_tokenizer=False.
A GPU is optional: the notebook selects cuda when available and cpu otherwise.
Code and the three released checkpoints are MIT licensed.

steps.title: Extract embeddings for a folder of structures
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from mulan.dataset import ProteinDataset, data_collate_fn_dynamic
from mulan.model import StructEsmForMaskedLM
from mulan.model_utils import auto_detect_base_tokenizer

protein_data_path = './example_structures'
saved_dataset_path = './example_dataset'
is_experimental_structure = False
use_foldseek_sequences = False

dataset = ProteinDataset(
    protein_data_path=protein_data_path,
    saved_dataset_path=saved_dataset_path,
    use_foldseek_sequences=use_foldseek_sequences,
    is_experimental_structure=is_experimental_structure,
)

model = StructEsmForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    'DFrolova/MULAN-small',
    device_map="auto",
)
device = 'cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
model.to(device)

esm_tokenizer = auto_detect_base_tokenizer(model.config, use_foldseek_sequences)

def data_collator(x):
    if use_foldseek_sequences:
        one_letter_aas = esm_tokenizer.all_tokens[5:]
    else:
        one_letter_aas = dataset.tokenizer.one_letter_aas

    return data_collate_fn_dynamic(x,
        esm_tokenizer=esm_tokenizer,
        nan_value=np.deg2rad(dataset.tokenizer.nan_fill_value),
        mask_inputs=False,
        all_amino_acids=one_letter_aas,
        use_foldseek_sequences=use_foldseek_sequences)

dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=1, shuffle=False, collate_fn=data_collator)

with torch.no_grad():
    for i, (batch, batch_names) in enumerate(zip(dataloader, dataset.protein_names)):
        struct_inputs = [struct_input.to(device) for struct_input in batch['struct_inputs']]
        embeddings = model(
            input_ids=batch['input_ids'].to(device),
            attention_mask=batch['attention_mask'].to(device),
            struct_inputs=struct_inputs,
            output_hidden_states=True
        )['hidden_states'][-1]
        embeddings = embeddings[0][1:-1]
        protein_embedding = embeddings.mean(dim=0)
        print(batch_names, embeddings.shape, protein_embedding.shape)
PY
